q: How does dropout work and why scale by 1/(1−p)?
a: During training each activation is zeroed with probability p, so the network can't rely on specific neurons; it's like training an ensemble of sub-networks. The kept activations are divided by (1−p) so their expected value matches inference, when dropout is off (inverted dropout).

BatchNorm normalises each feature across the batch and uses running statistics at inference; great for CNNs but depends on batch size and behaves differently in train vs eval. LayerNorm normalises across the features of each example/token; batch-independent and identical in training and inference, so it's the standard in Transformers and RNNs.

q: What happens if you forget model.eval() at inference?
a: Dropout stays on (random, degraded predictions) and BatchNorm uses the current batch's statistics instead of running averages (predictions depend on what else is in the batch). Also use torch.no_grad() to skip gradient tracking.

q: Why does BatchNorm struggle with small batches?
a: The batch mean and variance become noisy estimates with only a few examples, which destabilises training and creates a mismatch with the running statistics used at inference. Use GroupNorm or LayerNorm instead.

q: List ways to reduce overfitting in a deep network.
a: More data and augmentation, dropout, weight decay (AdamW), early stopping, smaller model, label smoothing, transfer learning from a pretrained model instead of training from scratch, and mixup/cutmix for images.

A simplification of LayerNorm that only rescales by the root-mean-square of the features (no mean subtraction, no β): \(x/\sqrt{\text{mean}(x^2)+\epsilon}\cdot\gamma\). Cheaper, works as well, used in LLaMA-style LLMs.
